author: Mariam Mayet
title: Who controls the food system controls the future
content:
Walk into any major supermarket in South Africa, and the shelves seem to tell a story of abundance: aisles of bread, meat, dairy, fruit, vegetables, cereals, snacks, and processed foods wrapped in the language of choice, convenience, and modernity. This food system is often held up as a model for the rest of the continent: modern farms, sophisticated logistics, powerful processors, dominant retailers, and the capacity to produce, import, export, and distribute food at scale.




Yet behind this display of plenty lies a brutal contradiction. Millions of working-class people are hungry, food prices are punishing, and child malnutrition and diet-related disease persist. While farm and food workers labour under exploitative, insecure, and often dangerous conditions, small-scale farmers struggle to survive.




The African Centre for Biodiversity’s (ACB’s) new report, 

The architecture of control: corporate power, financialisation, and democratic food futures in South Africa

, argues that this is primarily a problem of power. It is about who owns, controls, and profits from the food system; how corporate concentration shapes production, prices, markets, labour, and consumption; and how the state has retreated from its constitutional duty to guarantee the right to food, leaving corporations and financiers to decide what food future is possible.

author: Simon Ramapuputla
title: Cosatu congress adjourned after credential dispute exposes tensions
content:
The Congress of South African Trade Unions (Cosatu) has adjourned its 15

th

 national congress after seven affiliates withheld their delegate credentials, preventing the federation from reaching the quorum required to proceed with the meeting.




The decision, announced after two days of difficult proceedings, brought the congress to a halt before delegates could debate the federation’s political report, organisational matters and resolutions affecting workers.




Speaking to 

Elitsha

 outside the congress venue on Wednesday, Cosatu spokesperson Zanele Sabela said the decision by some affiliates not to submit their credentials was linked primarily to the suspension of Cosatu’s first deputy president, Mike Shingange, by his union, the National Education, Health and Allied Workers’ Union (Nehawu), shortly before the congress.




Sabela said the suspension had become a “bone of contention” because affiliates wanted clarity on why Shingange had been suspended on the eve of the congress and whether the move would prevent his candidacy for a leadership position. Nehawu’s general secretary clarified in the congress that the suspension was an internal union matter and did not mean Shingange could not stand for a Cosatu position. She said Shingange remained a shop steward and a member of an affiliated union.
